title: Microeconomics for Finance
text:
This course provides students with relevant microeconomic methods to tackle finance issues. The course covers 24 hours of material and is designed for first-year Master in Finance students at Paris Dauphine University - PSL.


The course consists of four main topics:

Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy - Understanding how markets allocate resources through voluntary exchange
Decision Making under Uncertainty - Expected utility theory and risk preferences
Equilibrium in Markets for Securities - Asset pricing and portfolio theory
Investment Decisions under Market Imperfections - Asymmetric information and agency problems






Topic 1: Exchange Economy
Understanding the fundamentals of market equilibrium with a focus on exchange between agents.


Topic 2: Decision under Uncertainty
Expected utility theory, risk aversion, and portfolio choice.


Topic 3: Securities Markets
Asset pricing models, CAPM, and market equilibrium concepts.


Topic 4: Market Imperfections
Asymmetric information, principal-agent problems, and real-world market frictions.






Instructor: Juan F. Imbet
Institution: Paris Dauphine University - PSL
Level: Master in Finance, 1st Year
Duration: 24 hours
Evaluation: Mid-term and final exams




By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Understand the fundamental concepts of microeconomic theory as applied to finance
Analyze market equilibrium under different conditions
Apply expected utility theory to decision-making under uncertainty
Comprehend asset pricing models and their implications
Recognize the impact of market imperfections on investment decisions





Basic knowledge of microeconomics
Familiarity with mathematical concepts (calculus, probability)
Understanding of financial instruments


This course builds upon the foundational work of previous instructors while incorporating modern developments in financial economics.

title: About
text:
Juan F. Imbet
Assistant Professor
Department of Finance
Paris Dauphine University - PSL



This 24-hour course in Microeconomics for Finance aims to equip students with essential microeconomic tools for analyzing financial markets and decision-making. The course bridges theoretical microeconomics with practical applications in finance.



Upon completion of this course, students will be able to:

Apply microeconomic principles to financial decision-making
Understand market equilibrium concepts in financial contexts
Analyze decision-making under uncertainty using expected utility theory
Comprehend asset pricing models and their implications
Recognize the impact of market imperfections on investment decisions




The course is divided into four main modules, each building upon the previous one:

Foundation: Exchange economy and basic equilibrium concepts
Risk and Uncertainty: Decision theory and risk preferences
Asset Markets: Pricing and portfolio theory
Real-World Applications: Market imperfections and agency problems




All course materials are provided in interactive HTML format using Quarto and Reveal.js, allowing for an engaging learning experience with embedded mathematical expressions and visualizations.



For questions about the course content or materials, please contact the instructor.



This course builds upon the foundational work of previous instructors and incorporates modern developments in financial economics and teaching methodologies.

title: Exercises: Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
text:
Adam and Bob are the only two individuals in an island. Adam has been able to collect 10 coconuts and 5 fish, while Bob has 5 coconuts and 10 fish. Both individuals have the same utility function over coconut and fish consumption bundles represented by the following Constant Elasticity of Substitution (CES) utility function: \[
u(X_c, X_f) = \left( X_c^{\frac{\sigma - 1}{\sigma}} + X_f^{\frac{\sigma - 1}{\sigma}} \right)^{\frac{\sigma}{\sigma - 1}}
\] where \(X_c\) is the number of coconuts, \(X_f\) is the number of fish, and \(\sigma\) is the elasticity of substitution between coconuts and fish. Assume that \(\sigma = 2\).

Compute the Marshallian demand functions for coconuts and fish for both Adam and Bob as a function of prices.
Compute the equilibrium prices of coconuts and fish in this economy.
Compute the equilibrium consumption bundles for both Adam and Bob.
For an arbitrary level \(\bar{u}\) of utility, compute the Hicksian demand functions for both Adam and Bob as a function of prices and utility.
Compute the expenditure functions for both Adam and Bob as a function of prices and utility.
Show that both demands coincide.




Only one hospital in a country provides medical services. Citizens have preferences over medical services and cash that they can use for their own spending. Cities have the following utility function:
\[
U(X,C) = X^{\frac{1}{2}} C^{\frac{1}{2}}
\]
where \(X\) is the number of medical services received, and \(C\) the amount of cash. Currently, the government has allocated 1 million services to city 1, and 2 million services to city 2. Cities have currently no cash. However, the government is thinking about implementing a policy in which cities can exchange medical services to other cities outside of this economy and receive 80% of the price of the services that they give away. If the normalized price of cash is \(1\), compute the total demand of services and cash for each city after this policy is implemented.



In the market for tobacco and alcohol, Carol and Dave have preferences represented by the following utility functions: \[
U_C(X_t, X_a) = X_t^{\frac{1}{3}} X_a^{\frac{2}{3}}
\] and \[
U_D(X_t, X_a) = X_t^{\frac{2}{3}} X_a^{\frac{1}{3}}
\]
where \(X_t\) is the number of tobacco units, and \(X_a\) the number of alcohol units. Carol has an initial endowment of 4 units of tobacco and 1 unit of alcohol, while Dave has an initial endowment of 1 unit of tobacco and 4 units of alcohol. Compute the Mashallian Demands.

Find the equilibrium prices of tobacco and alcohol in this economy.
Assume that the government has imposed a tax of \(20\%\) on tobacco consumption. What are the implicit transfers that the government has to give/receive to/from Carol and Dave to achieve an equilibrium? Think about the Second Welfare Theorem, these transfers do not need to be unique.
If the government only uses the collected tax revenue for transfers, what would be the transfers to Carol and Dave?




Apples and Pears are in season. Eve and Frank are the only market participants. They have agreed that the first \(\bar{A}\) units of apples will be sold/bought at a price of \(\bar{p_a}\) but every extra apple will only pay \(\frac{\bar{p_a}}{2}\). The same agreement has been made for pears, where the first \(\bar{P}\) units of pears will be sold/bought at a price of \(\bar{p_p}\) but every extra pear will only pay \(\frac{\bar{p_p}}{2}\). Eve has an initial endowment of \(\omega_{EA}\) apples and \(\omega_{EP}\) pears, while Frank has an initial endowment of \(\omega_{FA}\) apples and \(\omega_{FP}\) pears. Both individuals have the same utility function represented by the following Cobb-Douglas utility function:
\[
    U(X_A, X_P) = X_A^{\alpha} X_P^{1 - \alpha}
\]
where \(X_A\) is the number of apples, \(X_P\) the number of pears, and \(\alpha \in (0,1)\).

Compute the Marshallian demand functions for apples and pears for both Eve and Frank as a function of prices.
Compute the equilibrium prices of apples and pears in this economy.
Compute the equilibrium consumption bundles for both Eve and Frank.
How do the equilibrium prices and consumption bundles change if \(\bar{A}\) and \(\bar{P}\) increase?





For a two good (1,2), two consumer (A,B) exchange economy and initial allocations \[
\omega_A = (4, 2) \quad \text{and} \quad \omega_B = (2, 4)
\]
Assume that both consumers have the same utility function represented by the following Cobb-Douglas utility function: \[
U(X_1, X_2) = X_1^{\alpha} X_2^{1 - \alpha}
\]
Draw a 6 by 6 box in which the x-axis represents good 1 and the y-axis good 2. The bottom left corner represents the origin for consumer A (no consumption), while the top right corner represents the origin for consumer B. This is called an Edgeworth box, it’s like putting two coordinate systems one in top of the other.
As a point draw the initial endownment of both consumers.
Draw the equation representing the budget constraint for consumer A using its (0,0) point as a reference. Do the same for consumer B using its origin point as a reference.
For different values of \(\bar{u}\), the relation between \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) is called an indifference curve \[
\bar{u} = X_1^{\alpha} X_2^{1 - \alpha}
\]
For the first consumer, draw different indifference curves. What can you say about their shape?
What is the slope of the budget constraint?
Compute the equilibrium prices.
